chapter_note: The chapter opens with a formulaic dialogue frame, then preserves a substantial core cosmological teaching (Mother of Life; First Man) describing divine grief within the Light–Darkness conflict. The second half shows strong editorial fatigue: it shifts to Mani’s self-presentation and the suffering of the institutional “holy church,” then to a Christianized eschatological warning (gehenna/repentance), suggesting later community expansion beyond the older substrate.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Formulaic opening (“Once again… speaks to his disciples”) is characteristic hagiographic/frame apparatus; the whole sentence functions as an editorial setup for the chapter’s theme.

paragraphs.core_text: The first who grieves is the first Mother of Life. She is sad because of her children who are set in affliction, for they were conjoined with the Darkness and the [poi]son. They have been bound with the entire ruling-power. For what was she grieving, [wa]tching over them taking these afflictions? Whenever she might [s]ee them and how suffering is brought upon them, she shall grieve and be unhappy on account of them.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Impersonal cosmological exposition: a named Light power (Mother of Life) and her children’s entanglement with Darkness/ruling-power; no institutional application, no citation, no audience address.

paragraphs.core_text: [The s]econd one who is troubled of heart is the First Man, whose [great]ness and kingdom is established in the li[ght] ship [...]. And he too is troubled of heart because of his five sons who are set in the midst of danger. For any time he may see that they are given trouble, always he might hear the sound of their weeping as they cry out because of the blows and wounds of the enemy who assaults them daily; and as he sees them like this constantly, he shall g[ri]eve and mourn on account of his [s]o[n]s.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Core cosmology continues: First Man and his five sons (a systematic Manichaean structure) situated in cosmic geography (“light ship”); suffering described within the cosmic conflict rather than mapped onto church life.

Autobiographical Mani-first-person plus institutional identifiers (“holy church,” persecution by enemies, choosing the church) indicates later hagiographic/editorial self-positioning rather than the older impersonal substrate.

Soteriological warning framed in Christianized eschatological language (“gehenna,” repentance, reconciliation/peace-mercy). This reads as a later Christian overlay rather than a closed cosmological description of how the system works.
